articles.title: ‘The Dog Stars’ Review: Jacob Elordi’s Sensitive Survivalist Can’t Sustain a Dreary Dystopian Adventure
articles.summary: It’s the end of the world as we know it in “The Dog Stars,” and everyone feels — well, not fine exactly, but, you know, fine? Alive, hanging in there, taking...
articles.body:
It's the end of the world as we know it in "The Dog Stars," and everyone feels — well, not fine exactly, but, you know, fine ? Alive, hanging in there, taking it one day at a time. Things could be better, which goes without saying in the aftermath of a flu pandemic that has wiped out most of the planet's human population, but the four principals here could also be dead, so there's that. That shrugging, slightly bereft air of just-getting-by is the prevailing mood of Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic survival story, and it's a tough one to sustain dramatically, much less with any sense of intrepid adventure. Somewhat aptly released at the tail end of a long, loud movie summer, this is a surprisingly low-energy, low-incident blockbuster; you'd appreciate its mellow, character-oriented approach if it gave you any real characters to hold onto.

Peter Heller's popular 2012 source novel largely did. Concentrated and eventful, it brought Jack London-style terseness and lyricism, as well as some mordant gallows humor, to the oft-solitary saga of Hig, a qualified mechanic eking out a life on an abandoned airstrip in rural Colorado, less than a decade after the fateful plague. (The year in the film is given, most pessimistically, as 2035. Start stockpiling now.) On the page, Hig's first-person descriptions of his everyday adventures, and of the waning natural world around him, had an honest, melancholy soul to them. That voice doesn't carry over to the adaptation by screenwriter Mark L. Smith — something of a specialist in survivalist drama, having also scripted "The Revenant" and "The Midnight Sky" — which forgoes narration altogether; the film bets on Jacob Elordi's blokey, slightly sad-eyed charm to fill in the gaps.

It's not a bad bet; it just doesn't quite pay off. Elordi's gift as a performer is for mining deeper seams of humanity in unappealing characters, from the douchey trust-fund scion of "Saltburn" to the literal monster of "Frankenstein." Given a simply dull one, as he is here, he fares less well. The film's Hig is nice; he's admirably practical and resourceful; he looks terrific in weathered Carhartt workwear. But even handed the sympathetic accoutrements of a faithful German shepherd sidekick and repeated silent flashbacks to his deceased wife, he remains a bit of a blank. The film's strangely lackadaisical opening act, heavy on scenes of Hig flying his battered Cessna alone, desperately needs the gruff friction provided by Josh Brolin as Bangley, his fellow survivor turned reluctant platonic life partner.

Hig and Bangley have an established routine that keeps them alive, if not all that elated to be so. Hig regularly flies to Denver, now a bombed-out ghost town, to pick up supplies from sundry abandoned stores, bars and hospitals. On their compound, they alternate guard duty, on the alert for sporadic bands of intruders, whom Bangley insists be shot on sight. When Hig can't take it anymore, desperate for any kind of escape, he winds up crash-landing his plane near the spartan farm of grizzled rancher Jack (Guy Pearce) and his lonely daughter Cima (Margaret Qualley), whose routine is similarly, joylessly focused on existence and endurance: The grass, of course, is always greener on the other side of the Rockies. A thin romance ensues. The dramatic tempo stays much the same.

At its most interesting, "The Dog Stars" mimics the structure and stakes of a classic frontier Western, echoed quite literally in its two liveliest action setpieces: a briefly spectacular yet unperilous buffalo stampede, and a faceoff with a marauding tribe of feral, thickly made-up men on horseback, rather incuriously positioned by the film as an outright enemy force. The old-fashioned cowboys-and-Indians dynamic of this sequence is hard to ignore, as is the shared whiteness of the film's leading characters: In this dog-eat-dog world, whose brutal survival strategies get to be heroic, and why?

Smith's spare, episodic script doesn't risk such introspection, or indeed much else — save for one whopper of a departure from the novel, late in the proceedings, that sharply wrests the tone from ruggedly earnest wilderness drama to macabre, borderline-camp horror-comedy, only to reverse course so abruptly you wonder if either you or the film dropped out for a quick fever-dream. It certainly yanks your attention amid the generally homey, lolloping rhythm of the film. It also more or less demolishes whatever credibility this future-rustic story world has built up to this point. In this case, Scott's famously catholic genre interests come at some cost to the integrity of the whole enterprise; you sense he might feel as impatient with these sturdy, morose, faintly drab characters as we do.

All four stars ably play the stoic and sorrowful notes required of them, without finding many secondary or contrasting ones in their dialogue. "The Dog Stars" winds up coasting on their collective capabilities and charisma, as well as on Scott's autopilot proficiency. If the tirelessly prolific director never seems more than intermittently invested in this material, the strongest passages here thrive on his muscular command of scale, and he can still pick a landscape with the best of them: Northern Italy fills in robustly for the Centennial State here, even though Erik Messerschmidt's consistently charcoal-washed lensing suggests there's no magic hour in this unforgiving dystopia. This isn't a future to be prettified, and fair enough, but that impulse also falls in line with the film's stubbornly un-fun, eat-your-greens demeanor: Can't something here thrive rather than survive?

articles.title: Sandra Sá se conecta com o rap em EP motivacional, 'Indo pra dentro', que traz feats com King Saints e Davi Moraes | G1
articles.body:
Sandra Sá lança amanhã, quinta-feira, 27 de agosto, o EP 'Indo pra dentro' com sete músicas, sendo três inéditas e quatro regravações — Foto: Cristina Granato / Divulgação

♬ Em 1996, quando Sandra Sá lançou um dos mais coesos e sedutores álbuns de discografia que nem sempre esteve à altura da voz calorosa da cantora, “A lua sabe quem eu sou”, a artista carioca evocou a ancestralidade africana em uma das grandes músicas do disco, “Koo lei lei”, parceria da artista carioca com Kevin Mulligan.

É essa composição que encerrava o álbum “A lua sabe quem eu sou” – e que foi abafada na época pelo sucesso das gravações das músicas “Sozinho” (Peninha, 1996) e “Vamos viver” (Herbert Vianna, 1996) – que a cantora e compositora resgata, 30 anos depois, na faixa de abertura do EP “Indo pra dentro” em gravação de pegada afro que traz Marissol Mwaba e a rapper King Saints. “Não ando só / No meu sangue, carrego laços que dão os nós”, rima Saints no rap inserido em “Koo lei lei”.

Programado para ser lançado amanhã, quinta-feira, 27 de agosto, dia do 71º aniversário de Sandra Sá, com capa que expõe arte de Freddy Onirico, “Indo pra dentro” é disco situado na fronteira entre EP e álbum por reunir sete faixas gravadas com a alma funk soul da artista e com incursões pelo rap.

No disco, Sandra reforça os laços africanos em vibe positivista já traduzida no título, “Sou tão feliz” (Simone Malafaia, Sandra Sá, Bruno Gimenes e Patrícia Cândido), da música inédita que promove o EP “Indo pra dentro” em gravação que mistura soul, rock e rap – este novamente a cargo da rapper fluminense King Saints – e versos falados na voz grave de Sandra.

Com safra autoral de qualidade moderada, o EP “Indo pra dentro” soa como um chamado de união para a vida e para a luta – mote da música “Sobre viver [Cada linha]” (Sandra Sá, Simone Malafaia, Monica Odeh), outra inédita do disco.

Essa atmosfera de felicidade é acentuada pela regravação de “Dançando com a vida” (Sandra Sá, Zé Ricardo, Ana Lima e Gabriel O Pensador, 2000), música de outro álbum importante de Sandra, “Momentos que marcam demais” (2000). “Dançando com a vida” ganhou um toque de samba e versos falados na linha alto astral do EP, gravado com produção musical orquestrada pela própria Sandra Sá.

Parceria inédita de Sandra Sá com o guitarrista Davi Moraes e com Noé Ribeiro e Simone Malafaia, “Na pausa do compasso” tem batida funkeada e clima dançante à moda Black Rio, mas com beats contemporâneos. “Observa, absorva”, pedem Sandra e Davi, convidado da gravação, nos versos imperativos dessa faixa sobressalente no trio de músicas inéditas de “Indo pra dentro” pelo groove aliciante.

Música lançada pela cantora há 18 anos em gravação com os MCs Garrincha e Julinho, “Tem que acreditar” (Sandra Sá, Shayder, Julinho e Lidiane Madureira, 2008) é rebobinada no EP na mesma linha do funk com versos motivacionais que reforçam o traço de união sublinhado por Sandra nas letras desse repertório.

Fechando o EP “Indo pra dentro”, Sandra Sá regrava com certa vibração festiva a música “Movimento (Bagulho doido)”, parceria com Luiz Caldas e César Rasec apresentada pela cantora há 16 anos no álbum “Africanatividade – Cheiro de Brasil” (2010). A música é embasada pelo batuque miscigenado que tem a cara e o cheiro do Brasil.

Enfim, mesmo com baixo teor de novidade, o EP “Indo pra dentro” tem o mérito de trazer Sandra Sá – desde 2021 novamente sem o “de” que incorporara ao nome artístico em 1988 – de volta para o baile, agora em conexão com o rap, mas sem dissociar a cantora do funk e do soul, gêneros dos quais a artista é a primeira dama no Brasil.

articles.title: AI-generated music barred from Australian charts after Madonna cover controversy
articles.summary: SYDNEY, Aug 26 (Reuters) - AI-generated music will be excluded from Australia's music charts starting this week, the country's peak music trade group said, f...
articles.body:
SYDNEY, Aug 26 (Reuters) - AI-generated music will be excluded from Australia's music charts starting this week, the country's peak music trade group said, ‌following controversy over an Australian DJ's cover of Madonna's "Like a Prayer" ‌topping local music charts.

The Australian Recording Industry Association, or ARIA, said on Tuesday that wholly AI-generated tracks ​would no longer be eligible for its popular ARIA Charts, although recordings that use generative AI in a supporting role would remain eligible.

A recording developed using generative AI will be eligible only if it is "substantially human made" and raises no concerns ‌around streaming or chart manipulation, ⁠ARIA said.

To distinguish AI-generated recordings from AI-assisted ones, ARIA said it would apply definitions from a labelling standard announced by the ⁠global music community in July.

Major global record labels have been seeking new licensing arrangements to protect their vast catalogues as AI-generated music grows in popularity and consumers increasingly ​struggle ​to distinguish it from human-composed songs.

"The ARIA ​charts will always remain a transparent ‌measurement of the music Australia consumes, but a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent," ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said.

ARIA compiles Australia's most popular songs and albums in the ARIA Charts, which are released on Apple Music and Spotify every Friday.

Queensland-based ‌DJ Josh Fawaz's cover of Madonna's 1989 hit "Like ​a Prayer" became the most-played song on ​Australian radio and reached No. 4 ​on two ARIA charts in July. Some producers alleged that ‌generative AI had been used and ​that it was not ​initially disclosed.

Reuters could not immediately contact Fawaz for comment.

Responding to a music producer's criticism on Instagram in June, Fawaz said that although he used ​AI "as a tool, it's not ‌that deep", adding he had been releasing music long before AI ​and his focus was to provide his listeners "good music."

(Reporting by Renju ​Jose in Sydney; Editing by Stephen Coates)

articles.title: Paul McCartney Recalls Meeting Dolly Parton in 1970s Nashville, Shares Touching Tribute: ‘Such a Wonderful Woman’
articles.summary: McCartney shared the tribute amid the news of Parton’s death at 80 on Aug. 25
articles.body:
Paul McCartney shared heartfelt memories of meeting Dolly Parton at the Grand Ole Opry in the 1970s

McCartney praised Parton's unmatched talent, philanthropy, and business acumen in his emotional tribute following her death at 80 on Aug. 25

Parton's nephew announced her death months after she canceled her Las Vegas residency due to health challenges

Paul McCartney shared a heartfelt tribute to Dolly Parton following her death at 80 on Tuesday, Aug. 25.

McCartney, 84, shared two black-and-white photos taken by Jack Korn for The Tennesseean in 1974 in an Instagram post. The photos depict the pair of musicians first meeting, when McCartney and his late wife and Wings bandmate Linda McCartney visited Nashville to record the blues-rock influenced "Junior's Farm" and the country-tinged, fiddle-driven "Sally G."

In the photo, Parton can be seen greeting McCartney and his family, including daughters Heather and Mary.

"The magnificent star Dolly Parton has died and it is so sad," The Beatles alum began the tribute. "She was such a wonderful woman."

McCartney recalled first meeting the country icon at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, where she had been performing with Porter Wagoner . Parton would go on to pen her beloved emotional ballad " I Will Always Love You " about breaking from her musical partnership with Wagoner in 1974 in favor of pursuing a solo career.

"She was so bubbly and full of life it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed," McCartney added of Parton. "Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music and it is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly."

The musician also described the "Jolene" singer as "a very clever business woman who understood the value of her music and, most importantly, the effect that she had on the people of the world."

"There was no greater honour for me than to have her sing my song ' Let It Be ' and, even though I only made a small contribution to it, I am so honoured that she did it," McCartney added of her 2024 cover of The Beatles' 1970 hit for her album Rockstar. "I am so proud to have known her and admire her unique talents." "Thanks Dolly for the beautiful music you gave me and the whole world," he concluded. "We will always love you, god bless and rest in peace. You were the best."

Parton's nephew, Bryan Seaver, announced his aunt's death in an Instagram video on Aug. 25, months after the cancellation of her 2025 residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas due to "health challenges."

Parton's team later announced in a statement that her death came shortly after she was diagnosed with cancer .

"Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly's unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact," the statement read in part. "After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones."

In a November 2025 cover story interview, Parton opened up to PEOPLE about her then-upcoming 80th birthday, and her hopes for the remainder of her life and career, including her dedication to philanthropy, namely through her Imagination Library.

"I'm at that point in my life where I just want to be able to do good things that can be carried on," Parton told PEOPLE at the time. "I'm proud of my legacy so far, and I hope to just continue to do things that might be of use to other people."

articles.title: Appreciation: Dolly Parton was special to the LGBTQ+ community. She showed us our country loves us
articles.summary: Dolly Parton loved LGBTQ+ people, and we loved her — in part because she showed us that our country still loves us too.
articles.body:
In a brief online elegy for Dolly Parton , with whom she'd worked on the women-empowering film "9 to 5," actor and famed liberal activist Jane Fonda made it a point to note that Parton cared about her queer fans.

"To her gay and trans fans, I want you to know that she loved you," Fonda wrote. "You know that without me telling you."

Dolly meant something special to the LGBTQ+ community, in part because she represented an America where we are accepted — not just in big blue cities, but in one-room cabins in East Tennessee and in every rural, American-flag-flying corner of this big country.

Dolly was colorful and vivacious and unapologetic, and had more than a bit of drag queen in her. But she was also an unabashed ally with a country twang — a friend from the part of America where many queer people still instinctively put their guard up.

Of course, a country twang and queer acceptance can go hand in hand, and often do.

The Human Rights Campaign just last week cited a new U.S. Census Bureau analysis showing a record-high 12% of U.S. adults identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or gender diverse.

That's more than 25 million people, and they live all across the country. Many sound like Dolly. Many are surrounded by loving, supportive family too.

Yet it remained important, particularly as LGBTQ+ rights have come under increasing attack , that Dolly — big, beloved, down-home Dolly — had our back too.

She wrote and sang the Oscar-nominated song "Travelin' Thru" from the 2005 movie "Transamerica," about a transgender woman and her son. She collaborated with her goddaughter Miley Cyrus on "Rainbowland," a tribute to gay pride. And she made no secret of where she stood.

"I have some of everybody in my own immediate family and in my circle of employees. I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians," she said in 2023 . "I know and love them all, and I do not judge.… That's who they are. They cannot help that any more than I can help being Dolly Parton."

The LGBTQ+ community has watched in recent years as corporations and other supposed allies have backed away and gone quiet amid shifting politics and the Trump administration's war on diversity, equity and inclusion and the transgender community.

But not Dolly. We saw her stand her ground, next to us. And that meant something. Dolly showed that you can appeal to the whole of America without throwing LGBTQ+ people under the bus.

She showed that you can stand behind LGBTQ+ people without twisting into socially awkward or politically damaging positions, no matter your audience. Sometimes it just takes plain language about accepting everyone as they are.

She showed that holding onto faith, patriotism and the American way of life doesn't mean you can't also hold space for LGBTQ+ people to live their own happy lives.

She showed that we are all more alike than we are different, and that it's easier to see eye to eye when you aren't looking past one another.

Dolly showed that a country star and all-American icon, beloved as much in rural dive bars as big city queer clubs, could transcend the bogus narrative that LGBTQ+ lives are a political issue rather than a part of our collective humanity — and that all of us can too.

Dolly represented the America that LGBTQ+ people love and remain loyal to, the open-armed, diverse, compassionate, take-people-as-they-come version of America that is still all of ours to enjoy if we just work for it a little — just like Dolly did.

Dolly loved LGBTQ+ people, and we loved her — in part because she showed us that our country still loves us too.

articles.title: Dolly Parton Demonstrates How She Used Her Nails as an Instrument on the Set of “9 to 5” in Resurfaced 1981 Interview
articles.summary: “I’ve become famous for these nails,” Parton says in the clip
articles.body:
Dolly Parton used her acrylic nails to "get the rhythm" for the titular song on the set of 1980's 9 to 5

The country icon demonstrated the unique talent in a resurfaced interview clip from 1981

9 to 5 , which also starred Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda, marked Parton's acting debut

Dolly Parton was a woman of many talents.

The country legend, who died on Aug. 25 at age 80 , utilized her creativity on the set of her acting debut, the 1980 movie 9 to 5 .

In an extended 1981 interview on Sacramento's KCRA 3 , Parton demonstrated how she would rub her acrylic nails together to "get the rhythm" for the film's titular theme song.

"Ladies and gentlemen, you are now viewing the newest instrument on the market," she joked as she "played" her long red nails.

Parton explained that when she was writing the song on the movie's set, she used her nails "just to get the rhythm when I wasn't close to my guitar."

"It worked out good," she added. "So now, I've become famous for these nails."

Parton elaborated on her acrylic nail playing in an episode of Apple Fitness+ Time to Walk experience in 2021, sharing that her nails are actually credited on the 9 to 5 soundtrack.

"I thought this sounded like a typewriter, and since that movie was about women in the workplace, I'd stand on the set, I'd watch things happening, I'd come up with little lines every day," she said of writing the song. "I'd go back to my hotel room at night and get my guitar and put it down on tape until after a couple months I had a song."

She added that her nails are featured on the official recording of the song. "And I played my nails—even on the record it says 'nails by Dolly'!" she said. "Anyhow, everybody makes me do this all the time, play this little sound [of her nails like a washboard]. Of course you have to have acrylic nails, your own nails won't do that. You gotta have falsies!"

The star also shared that she had been offered several movie roles prior to 9 to 5 but turned them all down.

Jane Fonda approached Parton about the project knowing the country star would help drive a Southern audience to a movie with a mission of drawing attention to equal pay for women. With Lily Tomlin already signed on and Fonda, the film had "two big stars, so if it does good, I can take my part of the credit, and if it don't do good, I can just blame it on them," Parton recalled with a laugh. "Nobody knew me in the movies anyway!"

articles.title: Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson Named 2026 MacGuffin Award Honorees
articles.summary: Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson will be honored at the third annual MacGuffin Awards. The Property Masters Guild aims to highlight and elevate...
articles.body:
Luis Castro, Trish Reilly and Barry Wilkinson will be honored at the third annual MacGuffin Awards.

The Property Masters Guild aims to highlight and elevate the craft of the Property Master by raising awareness, fostering collaboration among craft artisans, educating its members and inspiring future generations of Property Masters.

'Weapons,' 'Marty Supreme' and 'Hacks' Among 2026 MacGuffin Awards Nominees

'The Bear,' 'Oppenheimer' and More Win Property Masters Guild Awards

The honorees, recognized for their craftsmanship, service and dedication within the property department and the broader production community in entertainment, were announced Tuesday.

Castro will receive the Humanitarian Award for his 25-year-long career in the food industry as an executive chef, private chef, culinary instructor and restaurant owner. Over the past decade, he transitioned into food styling for film and television, including "This Is Us," "Westworld," "9-1-1," "Bel-Air," "Paradise" and "Barbie." He also founded Imagine Cookin, an in-home cooking class company for neurodivergent individuals.

Reilly is set to take home the Presidents Award for her career as a food stylist on titles like "Obi-Wan," "Rebel Moon" and "The Orville," as well as the culinary creations of "Grotesquerie" and drinkable blood for "American Horror Story."

Wilkinson will be awarded the Lifetime Achievement Award after 40 years in the property department. He served as the property master of "Titanic," "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom," "Who Framed Roger Rabbit," two James Bond films including "GoldenEye" and all eight of the original Harry Potter films.

"The MacGuffin Awards are about recognizing the people whose creativity, generosity and dedication help define our craft, both on set and beyond it," said PMG President Jeffrey Johnson. "Luis, Trish and Barry each represent a different and invaluable part of what makes the property community so special. Their careers and contributions reflect the skill, ingenuity and spirit that we are proud to celebrate."

The third annual MacGuffin Awards will take place Sept. 12 at the Paramount Theatre in Hollywood. The live ceremony will also reveal winners in categories spanning film, television and commercial work.

articles.title: 'Batwara 1947' box office collection Day 12: Sunny Deol's film falls short of Rs 40 crore in India as it nears end of theatrical run, while 'Awarapan 2' races ahead, 'Toxic' to intensify competition
articles.summary: Sunny Deol-starrer 'Batwara 1947' arrived in theatres with considerable expectations, riding on the scale of the project, Aamir Khan's association as .
articles.body: Sunny Deol-starrer 'Batwara 1947' arrived in theatres with considerable expectations, riding on the scale of the project, Aamir Khan's association as a producer and Preity Zinta's return to the big screen. However, the film has struggled to translate that anticipation into box office success and is currently well short of recovering its reported budget.Batwara 1947 Movie ReviewDirected by Rajkumar Santoshi, the film opened with Rs 5.75 crore on Day 1 before witnessing a strong jump on Saturday, when it collected Rs 13.50 crore. The momentum did not sustain, with Sunday's collection dropping to Rs 7.25 crore and the first Monday bringing in just Rs 2 crore. 'Batwara 1947' eventually wrapped up its opening week with Rs 33.60 crore.The film has remained subdued in its second week as well. It added Rs 75 lakh on the second Friday, followed by Rs 1.15 crore on Saturday and Rs 1.30 crore on Sunday. The weekday collections have been particularly weak, with Day 11 bringing in only Rs 35 lakh. On the second Tuesday, Day 12, the film earned Rs 55 lakh.With these collections, 'Batwara 1947' has taken its India net total to Rs 37.70 crore. Given that the film was reportedly mounted on a budget of around Rs 120 crore, its current theatrical performance points towards a significant loss.The film's underwhelming run has also prompted trade analysts to examine why it failed to connect with audiences despite positive elements. Trade analyst Taran Adarsh recently shared his assessment with Bollywood Hungama, admitting that the film's failure surprised him.âWhat has really surprised me is why this film has not worked. In my opinion, it was a well-made film. I genuinely felt that the emotions between Shabana Azmi and Sunny Deol were very well captured on screen. The performances were of a very high order, while Rajkumar Santoshiâs direction was top-notch. The finale was very gripping. articles.title: Billy Ray Cyrus breaks silence on Dolly Parton's death with nod to rumored '90s affair
articles.summary: Billy Ray Cyrus has broken his silence in the wake of country superstar Dolly Parton's death with a moving tribute. See details.
articles.body:
Billy Ray Cyrus has broken his silence in the wake of country superstar Dolly Parton 's death with a moving tribute, even touching on the duo's rumored affair in the '90s when he was just breaking into the mainstream.

Dolly passed away on August 25 – which is also Billy Ray's birthday – at age 80, following a brief battle with cancer . She had dealt with several health issues in the last year of her life, particularly since the loss of her husband, Carl Dean , in March 2025.

Billy Ray took to Instagram to pay tribute to his late friend, who served as the godmother of his daughter, Miley Cyrus.

"I have so many moments and memories with Dolly, it's hard to know where to start. Like every little boy, I grew up loving Dolly Parton. She was a part of our lives, on our TVs, right in our living rooms," he wrote, alongside a carousel of photos of the pair.

"In 1992, I'll never forget walking into her dressing room to apologize for all the tabloid stories which claimed I was having an affair with her. In true Dolly fashion, she just looked at me, winked and said, 'Honey, this trash sells records!'" he continued.

"Dolly recently sent me a beautiful message, telling me she loved me with her whole heart. I will always love her in the same way…with my whole heart…and I always will," Billy concluded.

Learn more about Dolly's passing below...

Billy and Dolly met back in the '90s, and they became close friends after touring together.

"When Billy had the big song, 'Achy Breaky Heart,' well, we toured together. I was on tour, and then Billy toured with me, and so that's how we just got to be good friends, because he's a Kentucky boy, I'm from Tennessee," she shared on The Howard Stern Show .

Dolly Parton's heartbreaking cause of death revealed

Miley Cyrus' 'terrible habit' she learned from Dolly Parton, leading to new Hannah Montana special

Dolly Parton's legacy of kindness in her own words

Billy Ray asked Dolly to be Miley's godmother before her birth in 1992. "He said…'We're having a girl, and you've got to be her godmother!' And I said, 'Well, I'd be honored,'" the "Jolene" singer recalled on the show.

"So actually, Miley and I took over from there. We've just stayed very, very close through the years…I love Miley. She's my little sweetheart. I've known her since before she was born, actually."

Billy Ray shared insight into Dolly and Miley's close bond on AXS TV , revealing that the pair "actually just fell in love".

"Like it was kindred spirits. That sounds silly, but they were absolute. You could just feel it from the second they met. It was two peas in a pod."

Similarly, Miley has sung her godmother's praises time and again, including in an interview with TIME . "Dolly is not only my idol because of her incomparable career – she's also my role model because of her steadfast morals and values. At her core, she is the definition of a humanitarian," the "Flowers" singer wrote.

"Though she created an identity that she downplays as being built on wigs, lots of gingham and silicone, the foundation for this empire is actually her honesty, truth and her faith," Miley continued.

"People look to Dolly for guidance, and she knows that. She wears that responsibility with the same grace and pride she rocks a two-piece Nudie suit. She recognizes how impactful her choices will be as one of the most iconic and powerful voices in country music, and she leaves no one behind."

The Grammy winner concluded: "She's even better than your sparkliest dreams. She may be my fairy godmother, but I think she's that to everyone else too. I am happy to share her with the world."

articles.title: Dolly Parton's final words take on heartbreaking new meaning after her death at 80
articles.summary: The country legend spoke candidly about her late husband Carl Dean, her health struggles and the dreams
articles.body:
Dolly Parton was still dreaming about the future just four days before her death at the age of 80. The country music legend died peacefully in Nashville on Tuesday, August 25, following a brief battle with cancer , her team confirmed.

But in what would become her final interview, published by People on August 21, Dolly remained characteristically optimistic, speaking about the projects she still hoped to complete and insisting that, despite ongoing health struggles, she was "still working."

The poignancy of her words is even greater in light of her death just four days later. "You know me, as I've often said, I've dreamed myself into a corner and I still have so many things I want to achieve," she said, adding that she planned to keep working for as long as she could.

Dolly Parton's heartbreaking cause of death revealed

Who will inherit Dolly Parton's staggering $450 million fortune?

Dolly had been candid about experiencing health problems in the months leading up to her death, which had forced her to cancel several appearances and ultimately abandon plans for a Las Vegas residency.

In her final interview, the Jolene singer revealed that some of those problems had been neglected while she devoted herself to caring for her beloved husband, Carl Dean, before his death in March 2025.

"As I've shared in video messages throughout the past year, I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn't pay attention to when I was watching over Carl," she told the publication.

See the announcement of Dolly's death below...

Dolly acknowledged that it had been a difficult period, but typically refused to dwell on it. "It's not like I haven't been through hard times with my health," she said.

The singer also joked that speculation surrounding her condition had been amplified by the modern news cycle and social media, before making it clear she had no intention of quietly retiring. "Seriously, though, even though I'm still healin', I'm still workin'!" she said.

It was an outlook Dolly had maintained even as concern for her wellbeing intensified. In October 2025, following a public request for prayers from her sister Freida, she reassured worried fans in a video: "I don't think God is through with me, and I ain't done working."

Far from contemplating the end of her extraordinary seven-decade career, Dolly was still planning what came next.

She was working on the Life of Many Colors museum in Nashville, her SongTeller Hotel and her Broadway musical, Dolly: A True Original Musical, alongside a string of other ventures.

She also spoke excitedly about Cup of Ambition Coffee, a collaboration inspired by one of the most famous lyrics from her 1980 hit 9 to 5. The idea had been in the making for more than four decades, she revealed, adding that "some dreams take longer to come to life than others."

Even performing remained in Dolly's plans, although she admitted her days of traditional touring were behind her. "I definitely plan to do special performances in the future, but I won't tour anymore like I used to," she explained.

In typical Dolly fashion, she had even found a humorous solution, revealing that she was exploring the possibility of an avatar-based show in Nashville that could allow audiences to experience a Dolly Parton performance without requiring her to physically take to the stage. "I won't have to show up in person, but I still get paid!" she joked. "Sounds like a pretty good deal to me."

Dolly's enduring love for husband Carl Dean

Behind Dolly's determination to continue was an intensely difficult period in her personal life. Carl died in March 2025 at the age of 82, bringing to an end one of showbusiness' longest and most famously private marriages.

The couple first met outside the Wishy Washy Laundromat in Nashville in 1964, on the day an 18-year-old Dolly arrived in the city to pursue her dreams.

They married two years later and remained together for almost six decades, despite Carl largely choosing to stay away from the spotlight that surrounded his wife.

After his death, Dolly paid tribute to the man who had quietly remained by her side throughout her extraordinary rise from rural Tennessee to global superstardom.

"Carl and I spent many wonderful years together," she wrote. "Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years." She added: "Thank you for your prayers and sympathy."

The loss had a profound effect on Dolly, who later admitted that learning how to live without her husband was a significant adjustment. Her final interview makes clear that caring for Carl had also taken precedence over her own health.

Dolly's death was announced by her nephew Bryan Seaver, who also served as her longtime head of security. Her representatives subsequently confirmed that the music legend died following a "brief battle with cancer." A small private service will be held for her immediate family, with fans encouraged to donate to her beloved Imagination Library in lieu of flowers.

In a statement, her team remembered the singer's extraordinary life and the warmth that made her as beloved away from the stage as she was on it. "A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see," the statement read, adding that Dolly would remain an inspiration through her music, songwriting, "wit, warmth and kindness."

Her death came after a career spanning seven decades in which she became one of the most recognizable entertainers in the world, selling more than 100 million records and writing thousands of songs, including Jolene, Coat of Many Colors, 9 to 5 and I Will Always Love You.

articles.title: Kriti Sanon Rakhi ad: Giva jewellery drops Bollywood actor's Indian festival ad over outfit
articles.summary: Kriti Sanon has defended the ad in which she was seen celebrating the upcoming Hindu festival of Rakhi.
articles.body:
An Indian jewellery brand has removed their new advertisement for the upcoming festival of Rakshabandhan, also known as Rakhi, after backlash over the outfit worn by the female lead.

The ad featured popular Bollywood actor Kriti Sanon celebrating the Hindu festival in which sisters tie a thread called Rakhi over their brothers' wrists.

Sanon, who is seen in a cropped top, skirt and a drape, addressed her critics on Tuesday night saying "culture and traditions are in a woman's heart, not in her neckline!"

The row started earlier on Tuesday after actor and BJP MP Kangana Ranaut called the ad "intentionally creepy" and asked why someone would tie a Rakhi dressed in a bikini.

In her comments posted on social media, Ranaut did not name Sanon, but appeared to be referring to the actor.

"It is a wonderful time to be a woman, our closets are full of variety of clothes... From all the options that are available to us today why would you tie your brother a Rakhi in your bikini/under garments? Where are all your styling options? The advert looks intentionally creepy," she wrote.

Her remarks quickly drew attention online, with some users echoing her criticism of Sanon's outfit. One commentator described her top as a bralette, saying there was a "clear line between modern styling and basic sensitivity towards Hindu festivals".

"Pairing a bralette outfit with a sacred occasion like Rakshabandhan felt completely out of touch and unnecessary," she posted on X.

Others objected to a scene in the advertisement in which the actor also ties a rakhi on her pet dog.

But Sanon also received support, including from Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, who defended her, saying what a woman chose to wear was her own decision. Others accused Ranaut of moral policing.

Some also pointed out that though Ranaut has been more conservative in her clothing in recent years after becoming a politician, she herself often wore short dresses and Western outfits in her films and at social gatherings.

Sanon responded to the critics in an Instagram story, calling out the mindset that questioned women for their sartorial choices. Like Ranaut, she did not name anyone directly.

"The essence of festivals is not in the clothes you wear, it is in the emotions and meaning you hold for the traditions... When will we stop telling women what to wear?? Ethnic fashion has evolved over the years, but still a woman's respect for her culture is measured with just her clothes!! Culture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!"

Sanon also addressed the issue of tying Rakhi to her pet, saying though the festival traditionally celebrates the bond between a brother and sister, its spirit was about protecting loved ones - which, for her, included her sister and her pet.

Despite her spirited defence, jewellery company Giva announced on Wednesday it was pulling the ad.

"We have the highest regard and deep respect for Indian culture, traditions and festivals. As a brand, we have always believed in celebrating these joyous moments with the entire family and this time we wanted to extend the love and celebration to our pets," Giva said in a statement on Instagram.

"If our recent advertisement has inadvertently hurt the sentiments of some segments of society, that was not our intent at all. Out of respect, we have withdrawn the advertisement from all media," it added.

Giva is not the first Indian brand to withdraw an ad after criticism on social media. In 2020, popular jewellery brand Tanishq withdrew an advertisement featuring an interfaith couple after it faced right-wing backlash online.

Debates over what women should - and shouldn't - wear have also repeatedly sparked controversy in India.

Last year, a beauty pageant contestant was commended for standing up to a group of men who tried to bully her and other contestants over the skirts and western dresses they were wearing.

In 2021, there was outrage after a 19-year-old student, who turned up in shorts to take an exam, was forced to wrap a curtain around her legs after the teacher objected to her clothes.

In the same year, thousands of women - and some men - shared photos of themselves wearing ripped jeans after the chief minister of the northern state of Uttarakhand criticised a woman for wearing them.

articles.title: The wit and wisdom of Dolly Parton: 'If you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain'
articles.summary: The much-loved country singer-songwriter in her own words, following her death aged 80.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the much-loved US singer-songwriter who has died at the age of 80 , was known for her pearls of wisdom and humour as well as her music.

She regularly offered her perceptive and witty insights about life, music, fame and equal rights.

Here are some of her most memorable quotes from down the years:

"The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."

"I always just thought if you see somebody without a smile, give 'em yours!"

"I'm not going to limit myself just because people won't accept the fact that I can do something else."

"If you don't like the road you're walking, start paving another one."

"Don't get so busy making a living that you forget to make a life."

"Sometimes, what would look like to be my biggest mistakes turn out to be my biggest blessings."

"I actually take my songwriting more serious than anything else I do, so I would say I am a songwriter first."

"It's my way of expressing myself. It's my therapy."

"You have to search for a long time because I've written a lot of songs. But yes, there are pieces of me, of course, in everything I write."

"I have to write and sing. See, that was my first love, and I have to do that forever, however I have to do it."

"I look totally artificial, but I am totally real, as a writer, as a professional, as a human being. A rhinestone shines just as good as a diamond."

"My dream was always to make as many people happy as I could in this life."

"I always count my blessings, more than I count my money. I don't work for money, never did. It was the art, it was the job. I loved the work. And I've done well, and I'm thankful for it."

"I wanted more than to just be a farmer's daughter, even though I'm proud to be [one]. I just wanted pretty things. I wanted money to buy the things I had always been impressed with as a child. I wanted, I guess, to be a star."

"If I was trying to describe myself to someone that had never seen me before, I would say, 'Calm down. Don't get scared. It's just me. I know I look totally bizarre and artificial, but I'm totally real inside.'"

"I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb - and I'm not blonde either."

"It costs a lot of money to look this cheap."

"People always ask me how long it takes to do my hair. I don't know, I'm never there."

"If I see something sagging, bagging and dragging, I'm going to nip it, tuck it, and suck it."

"I don't like to be like everybody else. I've often made the statement that I would never stoop so low as to be fashionable. That's the easiest thing in the world to do."

"I make jokes about it, but it's the truth that I kind of patterned my look after the town tramp. I didn't know what she was, just this woman who was blond and piled her hair up, wore high heels and tight skirts, and, boy, she was the prettiest thing I'd ever seen. Momma used to say, 'Aw, she's just trash', and I thought, 'That's what I want to be when I grow up. Trash.'"

"I'm pretty sharp. I'm not educated and I'm not that intelligent, but I'm smart. They say somebody's street smart. I feel like if I got intelligence, it's just a country smart."

Journalist: "What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?" Dolly: "The fact that sometimes my mouth is a little too big and a little too open and sounds too much like a sailor."

"I'm very real where it counts, and that's inside."

"They say love isn't about two people gazing into each other's eyes, it is about two people gazing outwards in the same direction. I believe this with all my heart."

"I never really tried to hide myself from anybody. I think that's one of the reasons I'm still around, people feel like they know me."

"I don't want to be a star if I have no life."

Speaking more about the book gifting programme for children: "Since I had no kids and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom. So I think a big part of my success is the fact that I was free to work. And I didn't have children, because I believe that God didn't mean for me to have kids, so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like the Imagination Library."

"I ain't never gonna be old because I ain't got time to be old. I can't stop long enough to grow old. I'm just gonna be the best I can be at whatever age I am."

"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best. I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."

"When I die, I'll really be getting to live then because I believe that there is a greater place than this".

Journalist: "What would be her funeral song?" Dolly: "I don't know - but I won't be singing it!"

"Yes, I support gay marriage. They have every right to be as miserable as straight people."

"And of course black lives matter. Do we think our little white asses are the only ones that matter? No!"

"I've got transgender people. I've got gays. I've got lesbians. I've got drunks. I've got drug addicts - all within my own family. I know and love them all, and I do not judge."

"It's a good thing I was born a girl, otherwise I'd be a drag queen."

In a letter to young recipients of books from Dolly Parton's Imagination Library: "You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go."

She continued: "Just remember the lessons my family taught me - dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things and you can be anyone you want to be.

"You are terrific, and remember... I will always love you."

articles.title: Dolly Parton for beginners: How the Queen of Country wrote the playbook for Taylor Swift
articles.summary: Explore how Dolly Parton shaped the music industry and influenced artists like Taylor Swift, breaking barriers in country and pop music with her extraordinary talent, business acumen, and cultural impact.
articles.body: Dolly Partonâs status as the Queen of Country never quite explained the scale of her influence. A better measure came from Marshall Mathers, better known as Eminem, who after her death shared a handwritten note she had sent him following his induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Parton had congratulated him, admitted she knew little about rap and told him that he was âvery specialâ and touched people in ways he probably did not even realise.Eminemâs response said even more about her reach. âEven for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon. A superstar in every sense.â It was an unlikely exchange on paper: the blonde, rhinestone-clad queen of Nashville and the enfant terrible of Detroit rap. Yet that was precisely the point. Dollyâs influence had long escaped the boundaries of country music.After her death on August 25 at the age of 80 following a brief battle with cancer, the tributes stretched across generations and genres. Taylor Swift said a world without Dolly did not feel âpossible, real, or rightâ. Paul McCartney, Jane Fonda, Kacey Musgraves, Reba McEntire and Carrie Underwood were among those who mourned her. Eminem Stanned her.Dolly had stopped being merely a country star decades ago. She had become something closer to an American institution.The rags before the rhinestonesDolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946, the fourth of 12 children, and grew up in a one-room cabin in Locust Ridge in the Great Smoky Mountains. Her father, Robert Lee Parton, worked as a farmer and labourer and could not read or write. Her mother, Avie Lee, filled the house with songs and stories.Music became Dollyâs exit route. She was performing on local radio and television as a child, writing songs while other children were still learning multiplication tables, and appeared at the Grand Ole Opry at 13. The day after graduating from high school in 1964, she left for Nashville.âCoat of Many Colorsâ, one of her greatest songs, tells the story of a coat her mother stitched together from scraps. Dolly is proud of it until her classmates laugh at her.That is the trick in so many Parton songs. The language is simple, but the emotional equation is not. âCoat of Many Colorsâ is about maternal love, but it is also about class, humiliation and the moment a child discovers that other people can make poverty shameful.Porter Wagoner and the great escapeDollyâs breakthrough came in 1967 when Porter Wagoner recruited her for The Porter Wagoner Show. Wagoner was already a major country star; Dolly was the newcomer. Their television partnership made her famous, produced hit duets and gave her the platform from which her solo career could grow.Eventually, however, the protÃ©gÃ© outgrew the mentor.Dolly wanted to leave. Wagoner did not want her to go. So she wrote him a song.âI Will Always Love Youâ is now inseparable from Whitney Houston, whose 1992 version became one of the biggest singles in pop history. Dollyâs original is very different: quieter, smaller and more intimate. More importantly, it was not fundamentally a romantic breakup song. It was a farewell to Wagoner, telling a man she loved and respected that affection did not require permanent professional dependence.Then there was âJoleneâ. Instead of attacking the beautiful woman she fears may steal her man, Dollyâs narrator begs her. She admires Jolene almost as much as she fears her. Jealousy, vulnerability, fascination and desperation coexist inside one of country musicâs simplest melodies.How do you become the Queen of Country?Dollyâs distinction was that she made country portable.Her early catalogue established her as one of Nashvilleâs great storytellers. âJoshuaâ gave her a solo No. 1. âThe Bargain Storeâ turned emotional damage into the metaphor of second-hand goods still worth buying. âLight of a Clear Blue Morningâ captured the feeling of emerging from professional turmoil.Then âHere You Come Againâ pushed her decisively towards pop in 1977. She carried the accent, the hair, the humour and the Tennessee mythology with her.In 1980 came 9 to 5, opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin. Dolly played a secretary dealing with a sexist boss and also wrote the title song, turning the click of her acrylic nails into part of the rhythm.â9 to 5â became a No. 1 pop hit and a working-woman anthem. The casting was almost too perfect. Dolly had spent years being underestimated because she looked like exactly the kind of woman powerful men were conditioned not to take seriously. Now she was playing one.Three years later, âIslands in the Streamâ, her duet with Kenny Rogers, became another enormous crossover success. By then Dolly could move between Nashville, Hollywood and mainstream pop without ever appearing to be visiting any of them.Dolly IncThe most revealing Dolly Parton story may involve a song she did not allow Elvis Presley to record.Elvis wanted âI Will Always Love Youâ. His manager, Colonel Tom Parker, demanded half the publishing rights. Dolly refused. She kept the song, a decision vindicated when Whitney Houston turned it into a global phenomenon nearly two decades later.This is where the road from Dolly Parton to Taylor Swift becomes particularly interesting.Swiftâs battle over her masters involved a different part of music copyright, but the philosophy is remarkably similar: fame is useful, ownership is better. Understand what you have created, understand what rights attach to it and do not assume the men in suits know more about the value of your work than you do.Dolly understood that lesson when female performers were often treated as voices and faces attached to songs, contracts and catalogues controlled by other people.Dollywood turned her East Tennessee roots into a major tourist business. Dolly was a brand before celebrity branding became an industry.The woman behind DollyFor someone who made herself visually impossible to ignore, Dolly protected her private life with astonishing success.She met Carl Dean outside a Nashville laundromat on her first day in the city. They married in 1966 and remained together until his death in March 2025, nearly 59 years later.Dean wanted virtually nothing to do with show business. While Dolly became one of the most photographed women in the world, her husband largely stayed away from cameras, premieres and interviews.They had no children. Dolly instead became famously close to nieces, nephews and her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.The audience got Dolly Parton. Carl Dean got Dolly.From Dolly to TaylorThe line from Parton to Taylor Swift is not that Swift copied Dolly. It is that Dolly helped widen the space in which later female stars could operate.Both arrived in Nashville young. Both insisted that songwriting was central to their identity. Both crossed from country into pop. Both turned apparently conventional femininity into something commercially powerful rather than something for which they had to apologise. Both understood that control of intellectual property mattered. And both faced the strange assumption that a woman cannot simultaneously be a serious artist and an exceptionally clever businessperson.Dollyâs response to that problem was particularly ingenious.She exaggerated everything.The wigs got bigger. The heels got higher. The clothes got tighter. She joked constantly about cosmetic surgery and her appearance. Instead of trying to persuade people not to see a âdumb blondeâ, she gave them the most spectacular dumb-blonde costume imaginable and then quietly owned the songs, the publishing and eventually much of the business underneath the spectacle.That is perhaps her largest contribution to the women who followed her. She showed that femininity did not have to be surrendered to acquire authority. Her influence also travelled in less obvious directions. BeyoncÃ© could rework âJoleneâ, Miley Cyrus could inherit the mixture of country roots and pop spectacle, and Swift could turn songwriting ownership into part of her public mythology because Dolly had already demonstrated that a female star did not need to choose between commercial calculation, humour, glamour and artistic seriousness.The beginnerâs playlistIf you know Dolly but not the music, start with âCoat of Many Colorsâ for the storyteller; âJoleneâ for vulnerability; âI Will Always Love Youâ for the songwriter and businesswoman; âThe Bargain Storeâ for her gift for metaphor; âHere You Come Againâ for the crossover star; âLight of a Clear Blue Morningâ for independence; â9 to 5â for the working-woman icon; and âIslands in the Streamâ for Dolly at maximum mainstream wattage.Then go deeper into âJoshuaâ, âLove Is Like a Butterflyâ, âTwo Doors Downâ, âOld Flames Canât Hold a Candle to Youâ and her Trio recordings with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris.In 1995, partly inspired by her fatherâs inability to read, Dolly launched the Imagination Library, which mails free books to young children. It eventually expanded across several countries and distributed hundreds of millions of books.That may be why the mourning extended so far beyond Nashville.Dolly Parton spent a lifetime looking artificial and being remarkably real. She escaped poverty without disowning where she came from, escaped Nashvilleâs restrictions without abandoning country, crossed into Hollywood without giving up songwriting and turned a deliberately exaggerated image into armour.Most importantly, she understood the difference between fame and power. Fame was having everybody recognise the hair. Power was owning the song.Give your child the gift of confidence! Claim your exclusive TOI Masterclass spot today!

articles.summary: Royal experts say Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will likely "lay low" when Prince George starts at Eton College this September.
articles.body: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are expected to steer clear of releasing photos, making comments or generating other news that could overshadow Prince George’s highly anticipated first day at Eton College, according to a royal expert. "The Sussexes have assured the King that they will not hijack or derail major royal events, notably the first day of school term for Prince George at Eton," royal broadcaster Neil Sean told Fox News Digital. "By that, no pictures or comment from either one on that day in September." A representative for Archewell told Fox News Digital: "This is not something we would comment on." Kensington Palace did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.  The reported understanding comes as the Prince and Princess of Wales prepare for a major family milestone. Kensington Palace confirmed in June that George, 13, will attend Eton beginning this September, following in the footsteps of both his father, Prince William, and his uncle, Harry. PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON WRESTLED WITH MAJOR DECISION OVER PRINCE GEORGE'S FUTURE: EXPERT Royal commentator Amanda Matta told Fox News Digital that George’s arrival at the prestigious boarding school carries significance beyond a typical first day. "Prince George’s start at Eton isn’t just a personal milestone; it’s the beginning of his public-facing path as heir to the throne," Matta said. "The Palace is incredibly protective of that narrative, and any competing headline — especially one involving Harry and Meghan — threatens to distract from the ‘steady, future-focused’ brand the Prince and Princess of Wales have worked so hard to build." PRINCE WILLIAM ‘BLINDSIDED’ BY HARRY, MEGHAN RETURN AS KATE FEARS NEW TURMOIL FROM ROYAL FEUD: EXPERTS She added that, while the matter may not weigh heavily on Prince William and Kate Middleton personally, it could be important to palace staff working to keep the focus on the future king. They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story." GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE The spokesperson confirmed that the couple’s businesses will remain unchanged and based in the U.S. Meghan and Harry will also keep their home in California. "The Sussexes generate headlines simply by existing in public space," she said. "That’s been true since 2018 and hasn’t changed with their location or job titles." PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE'S UK RETURN SIGNALS ‘SPECTACULAR DEFEAT’ AS ROYAL EXPERTS WARN OF WILLIAM SHOWDOWN "If they also want to avoid collisions, it would require a level of coordination with the Palace that seems very unlikely given the current climate," she said.
